title: ITU Council 2026: State of the Union address by Doreen Bogdan-Martin, ITU Secretary-General
transcriptText:
Mr. Chair,
excellencies, fellow elected officials,
distinguished delegates and friends,
we meet at a moment of profound
transformation.
The world is more connected than at any
time in history.
But it is also more fragmented, more
uncertain and more divided in terms of
how that connectivity turns into
opportunity.
It is precisely in moments like this
that institutions must be resilient
and that the work we do here as one ITU
matters more than ever.
Three years ago, I stood before you for
the first time as secretary general and
promised a fit for future ITU built on
our collective vision and three pillars
of transformation.
In previous State of the Union
addresses, I presented our achievements
under the first two pillars,
strengthening ITU's position on the
global digital agenda, and second,
building a solid network of strategic
partners to advance universal meaningful
connectivity and sustainable digital
transformation.
This year as we approach the plenty
potentiary conference I will focus on
the third pillar building an ITU that is
recognized for its organizational
excellence.
An ITU that is agile,
open and transparent, more innovative,
financially stable, trusted and
resultsdriven.
Amid a digital landscape moving faster
than ever, it is now better equipped to
adapt and respond. Artificial
intelligence has helped us to become
more agile across our operations
starting with translation where
artificial intelligence has supported
expanded access to multilingual content
and contributed to efficiency gains of
up to 20%.
We are now automating in areas across
finance, HR and event management. As a
result, delegates will enjoy a modern AI
enabled experience at upcoming ITU
events, including AI for good, the WIS
forum, and the plenty potentiary 2026.
You'll see just outside this room live
demos of these improvements, and I hope
you will stop by to um see how they can
impact your work.
We are also making good progress towards
a union that holds itself to the highest
standards of accountability and
transparency.
Today, a fully staffed oversight unit
combining audit, investigation, and
evaluation functions is now operational.
We have a new independent umbbudsman
function which is shared with WIPO and
together with the ethics office and
oversight we have the capacity to
sustain that openness and transparency.
ITU is now an organization where
innovation comes from everywhere. Today
we have over 100 staff that have
graduated from our changemakers program.
Their work has helped to update our
recruitment processes, reinforced
evaluation, informed our AI use policy,
and led a new AI powered search tool
that we're excited to showcase at the
plannot 2026.
We have also evolved the head of IS
role. I think our head of I is in the
room into a chief information officer
who's working closely with the
transformation team to embed innovation
right across the ITU
counselors.
ITU is an organization that lives within
its means and makes every Swiss Frank
work harder for you and for all our
members. We have closed 2025 with a
budget surplus and savings have been put
forward for your consideration along
with plans to reinvest these savings
back into the union that delivers more
for its membership. We have achieved, as
the chair just alluded to, full Ipsis
compliance with improvements to Treasury
extra budgetary funds and budget
allocation systems. And we bring you a
balanced budget proposal which includes
global reductions for 2026 2027 period
as well as tighter controls on spending
and efficiency measures.
In recognition of continued economic
pressure on many ITU member states, we
continue to refrain from proposing an
increase in the contributo unit which
has remained, as you know, unchanged
since 2006.
In over three years, we have built a
union that the world can count on as a
trusted partner. Our membership has
continued to grow and also to diversify
and we are on track to welcome more than
400 new memberships during this cycle.
Between 2024 and 2025, ITU entered into
around 300 partnerships and I think
these are encouraging indicators of the
trust that stakeholders worldwide are
placing in us to advance our strategic
goals.
This trust was also reflected when the
UN General Assembly adopted the
resolution that culminated in the WIS
plus20 review. That resolution affirmed
ITU data as the gold standard for
tracking global digital development
progress and shows confidence in our
ability to provide evidence needed for
informed digital policy and investment
decisions. Last year marked the 80th
anniversary of the United Nations and
with it began a systemwide
transformation called UN80 to build a
stronger more effective United Nations
that did that delivers tangible results
to the people that we serve. As part of
these UN80 reform efforts, ITU was
entrusted to lead work packages on
technology and developing an expertise
on demand mechanism. Work that directly
informs our own review of ITU's regional
presence. Expertise on demand is going
to enable us to deliver specialized
knowledge more efficiently without
requiring our physical presence in every
location.
This reduces duplication and it
strengthens our overall impact on the
ground. We are proud that we have been
asked to lead these as aspects of the UN
reform and we take it as a recognition
of the impact of our own transformation.
In three years, we have moved from
tracking activities to measuring
outcomes. The strategic plan
implementation report that is before
this council shows our progress against
the goals that you set in Bucharest.
That same approach has us delivering on
longerterm commitments, including
getting our new headquarters project
back on track with minimal disruptions
to business continuity so that we can
keep driving results. And I would like
to thank member states for being so
constructive during that process. Thank
you. Thank you to MSAG and of course,
thank you to our host country of
Switzerland.
counselors, there is more to do in each
of the six areas of progress that I have
mentioned and we will continue to
deliver results through transformation.
But as you know, transformation is more
than reconfiguring an organizational
chart. It's driven by people, department
by department, team by team, colleague
by colleague. That's why I'm glad to
report ITU staff are upskilling,
adapting, and learning new tools using
time. We're encouraging at least eight
hours per month. And we're also offering
a space for innovation. By now, I hope
you have seen our new innovation hub, a
place where staff can experiment, where
they can try new ideas, where they can
share successes, but also failures in a
safe space.
Colleagues, transformation also depends
on a healthy and energized workforce.
And that's why we're implementing the
ITU wide action plan with targeted staff
wellness initiatives and outcome of last
year's staff engagement survey. I do
want to express my sincere appreciation
to the staff council for all of their
hard work and dedication to staff
wellness over the past three years.
We have also been glad to see the first
cohort of young professionals and you'll
be meeting them throughout the course of
this council. Our first cohort of young
professional young professionals really
brings fresh energy and new perspectives
to every corner of this union. And I
thank all the member states that have
supported this YPP program. Thank you
for helping us to invest in the next
generation of ICT leaders and the next
generation of ITU staff.
We also took time last year to recognize
the contributions of more than 200 ITU
staff. 200 ITU staff that had served
this great union for more than 20 years.
They are proof that institutional
resilience is ultimately delivered by
people.
Ladies and gentlemen, our transformation
journey is delivering results in the
wider world that we serve. It's a world
that increasingly depends on
well-coordinated spectrum, on safe and
sustainable space environments, on
interferencefree
radio communication services. And here I
want to acknowledge Mario Manuvich, the
radio communications director, and his
team. Mario has been leading this work
for more than a decade. I think uh under
his leadership, the ITU radio
communications bureau steered a
successful WRC 2023 in Dubai,
managed
3,62
to be precise frequency filings between
2023 and now. Some of some of those
filings, as you can imagine, contain
tens of thousands of satellites. And now
the radio communications bureau with all
of you is preparing for the WRC 2027
with a very spaceheavy agenda covering
things like direct to device, lunar
communications, and much much more.
Mario, thank you for everything you have
done for ITU.
Ladies and gentlemen, turning back to
resilient digital infrastructure which
is the theme of world telecommunications
and information society day. Our
international advisory body on submarine
cable resilience which was co-chared by
Nigeria and Portugal is successfully
concluding its work following this
year's Porto summit which resulted in
practical non-binding guidance to
strengthen the protection of submarine
cable infrastructure worldwide and chair
I want to thank you for your leadership
as co-chair of that advisory body.
I also want to recognize the deputy
secretary general Thomas Lmanowskis for
his leadership in digital resilience
from submarine cables to green digital
action in line with the WTISD theme of
digital lifelines. This includes an
expert report on critical digital risks
that we look forward to sharing with all
of you next week and also spearheading
our work on digital infrastructure
investment including a catalyzer that we
launched last year with our partners at
UMTAD at the financing for development
conference in Cibby.
Ladies and gentlemen, just weeks ago,
the world watched in awe, at least I
did, in awe as the Aremis 2 mission
orbited the moon using spectrum
coordinated by ITU.
The astronauts even streamed 4K video
from lunar orbit encoded with the H.265
265 standard developed by ITUt and
showing what global collaboration on
standards and spectrum makes possible.
Here I want to acknowledge our TSB
director Seo and Sunan and his team.
Seo's leadership delivered a successful
WTSA 2024 in New Delhi and under his
direction the ITU has strengthened its
collaboration with other international
standards development organizations.
ITUT is now at the center of global work
on AI standards from watermarking to
deep fake detection and multimedia
authenticity
and combined ITUt and ITUR approved more
than 1,000 standards during this cycle
shaping technologies from quantum to
next generation media
counselors resilient digital
infrastructure ure means nothing if it
cannot reach people, the people who need
it most. And here I want to acknowledge
our BDT director Cosmos Zabazava and his
team who delivered a successful WTDC
2025 in Baku last year. We thank the
amazing host from Azerbaijan
and that WTDC was held under the theme
universal, meaningful and affordable
connectivity for an inclusive and
sustainable digital future. That
conference not only translated global
digital development aspirations into
concrete regional initiatives and action
plans, but it also recognized the
importance of safeguarding public
telecom networks essential to
humanitarian services during armed
conflicts and disasters.
Councilors, the plenty potentiary 2022
adopted resolution 191 on intersectoral
coordination asking us to deliver as one
ITU. I would like to highlight very
briefly some of our collective
achievements that have been accomplished
with this one ITU spirit.
By the end of 2025, global internet use
reached 74%
with 6 billion people online, more than
ever before in history. Our digital
transformation spearheaded by BDT reach
more than 610,000 people between 2022
and 2025, and over half of them were
women.
Just last week, we celebrated Girls in
ICT Day, an initiative that has inspired
girls the world over to consider
studying STEM fields and consider
careers in the tech sector. We've helped
nearly 30 countries develop national
disaster preparedness roadmaps and
globally 60% of countries are now
covered by multi-hazard early warning
systems which is a testament to our
progress on early warnings for all. Our
Giga initiative with UNICEF has mapped
more than 2 million schools in over 140
countries, helping specifically 49
countries and territories bring their
schools online.
Our AI skills coalition, working closely
with the ITU Academy, has expanded
access to AI education for tens of
thousands of learners with 180 courses
in 13 languages. now available.
Our partner to connect digital coalition
has mobilized more than 80 billion US
dollars in commitments across over 1,000
pledges in 149 countries. And I do want
to thank everyone in this room that has
made a pledge. And if you haven't done
so yet, please, it's not too late. Feel
free to make a pledge. We have also,
ladies and gentlemen, scaled our field
presence to support more than 140
countries with digital policy and
technical assistance. And we look
forward to this council's discussions on
regional presence.
But ladies and gentlemen, numbers only
tell a part of the story. Last November,
I traveled to the Farana refugee camp in
Chad. What I saw there is something I
cannot forget.
Families who had lost everything. Young
people who watched their schools, homes,
and cities disappear.
But in the middle of that settlement
stood a connectivity center built in
partnership with UNHCR and GSMA. And
inside were young refugees accessing
education,
reaching family members across borders,
and beginning piece by piece to rebuild
a life. That's what a digital lifeline
can actually look like. A room with an
affordable internet connection and a
future being built inside it.
It's work on connectivity for refugees
is now active in Chad, Ethiopia, Uganda,
Moritania, Egypt, and Rwanda, advancing
towards our goal of connecting 20
million forcibly displaced people by
2030.
counselors. Everything I just described
takes sustained effort, investment, and
political will.
And pressures on all three are
intensifying.
We know from experience that resilience
is not a permanent state. It's a
practice. And it's a practice that is
being tested now more than ever.
But it's also never been more needed at
a time when 2.2 2 billion people remain
completely offline. At the same time,
multilateral institutions continue to
face the strong headwinds of funding
cuts and questions about relevance.
But when the cost of cooperation feels
high, I would urge you to think about
what could happen without it.
Uncoordinated spectrum resulting in
services being unusable. Unimplemented
standards resulting in higher cost and
technologies that cannot interoperate.
Unadressed digital divides becoming
AIdriven inequalities.
The case for multilateralism, ladies and
gentlemen, in our sector has never been
clearer. Technology is moving faster
than policymakers can keep pace, which
is why we must take must take every
opportunity to close the gaps. And one
is coming in just two weeks when
regulators are going to be gathering in
Anchora for the GSR 2026 and they will
be navigating the evolving digital
frontier together. The upcoming World
Telecommunication ICT policy forum and
NASO will be convening stakeholders to
build consensus on the emerging
technology questions that will shape our
next strategic cycle. And I want to
commend the informal expert group which
met here this past Sunday. I want to
commend that group for concluding its
work with a forward-looking
consensus-based set of opinions for the
forum to consider. And in July, ladies
and gentlemen, the first ever UN global
dialogue on AI governance, which ITU has
been entrusted to co-coordinate
alongside UNESCO.
That dialogue will take place together
with AI for good and the whises forum
back-toback here in Geneva. I think that
also reflects the trust that we have
built in digital cooperation around
artificial intelligence grounded in
years of thought leadership in this
space. Together they will mark a
defining moment and a meaningful shift
towards practical outcomes and broader
inclusion.
councilors, in just over six months, we
will gather in Doha for the plenty
potentiary conference to set the
direction the direction for the next
four years of this union's work. The
strategic plan implementation report
before this council will help us to
understand what worked, what needs
strengthening, what must we prioritize
in the next strategic period. But as we
close this cycle and look to the next
one, we know that resilience is not
sustained through austerity alone, but
reinforced through strong efficiency
measures and reinvesting in what
matters.
That is what continued resilience
demands and how it not only becomes but
remains fit for the future.
Ladies and gentlemen, Mr. chair. This is
the state of our union. A union that
made promises three years ago and
continues to deliver. A union whose
internal transformation strengthened
external resilience for institutions,
for networks, for people, and for
communities who need us most. A union
that is cleareyed about the challenges
ahead and strong enough to meet them.
The ITU has endured for 161 years
because every generation that came
before us understood that technology
only serves humanity when we decide and
when we organize ourselves to make it
so. From our inception, this
organization has evolved with every new
technology,
kept pace with each new wave of change,
and continues to do so today.
The case for what comes next is built on
what this union together has already
shown it can do. And I look forward to
continuing that work together as we
build a meaningfully connected,
sustainable digital world for everyone
everywhere. Thank you.
